passage:
Francis slammed the door so hard the calendar fell off the wall.
'Whoa,' his sister Ankita said from the sofa. 'What happened?'
'Neil happened.' Francis threw his bag down. 'I told him ONE thing. About liking Sara. He swore he'd never tell. And today he put it in the class group. With a heart emoji. Everyone saw.'
'Oh no.'
'Everyone laughed when I walked in. Sara wouldn't even look at me.' His voice cracked. 'I want to punch the wall.'
'Punch a cushion instead,' Ankita said, handing him one. 'And be as angry as you need. He broke a promise. That's a real thing to be furious about.'
Francis sat down, cushion crushed against his chest. 'I've trusted him since Class 3.'
'I know,' she said. 'That's why it hurts this much.'

qa.q: What did Neil put in the class group?
qa.a: He put in that Francis liked Sara, with a heart emoji.

qa.q: What is Francis feeling when his voice cracks?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and furious, and underneath deeply hurt that a friend since Class 3 broke his promise.

qa.q: Why is Ankita's response helpful at this first stage?
qa.a: She treats his anger as a fair reaction to a broken promise, offers a safe outlet, and doesn't rush him to calm down or forgive.

qa.q: What might Sara be experiencing after the post?
qa.a: Sara may feel embarrassed and put on the spot, which may be why she wouldn't look at Francis.

grounding: It shows a teenager raging after a close friend shared his secret, with his sister treating the anger as a healthy response to a crossed boundary.

passage:
It's been a month now, and I can finally write about it without my hands shaking.
I had told Madhav, and only Madhav, that my parents were fighting a lot and might separate. We were on his terrace, and he said, 'Your secret's safe, Darshan.'
Two days later, at the bus stop, a boy from 10C asked me, all fake-sad, 'Is it true your parents are divorcing?' Madhav was standing right there. He didn't even look embarrassed.
I remember the heat rising up my neck. I wanted to scream. I walked home fast instead and threw my cricket bat across the room so hard it left a mark on the wall.
Back then I thought being that angry meant something was wrong with me. Now I think it just meant something real had been broken.

qa.q: Where was Darshan when a boy from 10C asked about the divorce?
qa.a: Darshan was at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling as the heat rose up the neck?
qa.a: Darshan felt rage and humiliation at the secret being exposed, made worse by Madhav standing there unbothered.

qa.q: What insight about anger does Darshan reach looking back?
qa.a: That the anger wasn't a flaw but a sign that something real had been broken, a healthy first response to betrayal.

qa.q: What would have changed if Madhav had kept the secret?
qa.a: Darshan could have had a safe place to talk about the fights at home, instead of feeling exposed and alone.

grounding: It shows a teenager's rage and humiliation after a close friend revealed a family secret, and later seeing that anger as a sign a boundary was crossed.

passage:
Nirmala,
I'm writing this and I'm probably never sending it.
I told you about Papa losing his job because you're my best friend. I told you in your room with the door shut, and you promised. And today at lunch Rohit said, loudly, "Hey Asif, heard your dad's selling vegetables now?" and everyone laughed. You were sitting right there. You went red and looked at your plate. So I know it was you.
I've never been this angry. My hands are still shaking as I write. I wanted to throw my tiffin across the canteen. I wanted the ground to open up. I felt like everyone could see right through me.
Mummy says anger means someone crossed a line. Well, you crossed it. You took the thing I trusted you with and handed it round like a joke.
I don't know what I'll say to you tomorrow. Right now I just need you to know how much it hurt.
Asif

qa.q: What did Rohit say loudly at lunch?
qa.a: Hey Asif, heard your dad's selling vegetables now?

qa.q: What does Asif feel writing this letter?
qa.a: Asif feels furious and humiliated, hands shaking, betrayed by a best friend who shared the secret.

qa.q: What could Asif do with this anger tomorrow?
qa.a: Treat it as a sign a boundary was crossed, calm down first, then tell Nirmala honestly how much it hurt, or talk it through with Mummy.

qa.q: What might Nirmala be feeling when she goes red at lunch?
qa.a: Nirmala likely feels ashamed and guilty, knowing she broke Asif's trust.

grounding: A teenager whose best friend spread a private family secret feels rage and humiliation, and anger shows a line was crossed.

subtype: Stage 1: The hurt and the anger [Actor]
passage:
Abhinav bhaiya, stop laughing, it's not funny. Okay, fine, you think I'm overreacting. I'm not.
Megha was my best friend. Was. In March I told her that I still sleep with Bholu, my old stuffed elephant, when I'm stressed. I told her because I trusted her. Today, in the class group chat, she posted a photo of an elephant with "guess who can't sleep without this?" Thirty-two laughing replies.
I've never felt so small. I wanted to disappear. And then, on the bus, I felt something else: this huge hot anger, as if my chest was on fire. I've been angry for three hours.
Mummy says the anger is telling me something. That Megha crossed a line, and it's okay that it hurts.
So don't tell me to calm down. I'm Usha, and today I'm allowed to be furious. Tomorrow I'll decide what to do.

qa.q: What is the name of Usha's stuffed elephant?
qa.a: Bholu.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling on the bus?
qa.a: Usha felt a huge hot anger after the humiliation, as if her chest was on fire.

qa.q: What is wise about Usha deciding to wait till tomorrow?
qa.a: It honours the anger as a sign a boundary was crossed while giving time to cool before choosing how to respond.

qa.q: How might Abhinav be seeing his sister's anger?
qa.a: Abhinav may have found it funny at first, but is coming to see how hurt and humiliated his sister is.

grounding: A teen whose best friend exposed a private secret in a group chat feels humiliation and fierce anger, which her mother calls a healthy signal.

subtype: Stage 1: The hurt and the anger [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Yogesh told Shankar, his closest friend since Class 3, that he was scared of deep water and had faked a cold to skip swimming. "Don't tell anyone," he said. Shankar crossed his heart.
Tuesday. At the pool, the PE teacher called Yogesh forward. Before he could speak, Shankar shouted from the bench, "Sir, he's scared of water!" The whole class turned. Someone made chicken noises. Yogesh's ears burned so hot he thought they'd catch fire.
Wednesday. He didn't speak to Shankar at all. When Shankar tried to sit beside him in maths, Yogesh moved desks. Rage buzzed in him all day, loud and bright. At home he punched his pillow until his arms ached.
Thursday. His grandmother found him scowling at dinner. "Angry?" she asked. He nodded. "Good," she said, surprising him. "It means you know you deserved better. Now eat, and tomorrow we'll think about what to say to him."

qa.q: What did Shankar shout from the bench?
qa.a: Sir, he's scared of water!

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when the class made chicken noises?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and furious, his ears burning, betrayed by his closest friend.

qa.q: Why is the grandmother's response helpful?
qa.a: She treats his anger as a healthy sign that he deserved better, then helps him plan what to say instead of acting on it.

qa.q: What might Shankar feel when Yogesh moves desks?
qa.a: Shankar may feel rejected and guilty, realising how badly his shout hurt his friend.

grounding: Over a week a teen whose friend revealed his secret feels rage and humiliation, and his grandmother calls the anger a healthy first response.

subtype: Stage 1: The hurt and the anger [Actor]
passage: "Tanuja, your face is exactly like mine was at fifteen. Sit with your Zubin Mama and listen. My best friend then was Behram. We shared everything. One evening I told him I was scared of the dark, still, at fifteen. The next morning, the whole class was making ghost noises at me. Behram was laughing with them. I remember my ears burning, my hands shaking. I wanted to throw my geometry box at him. I didn't; I walked out and sat behind the school water tank until the bell. My mother found me angry at dinner and said, 'Good. You should be angry. He broke your trust.' That surprised me. I thought anger was wrong. It wasn't. It was telling me something important had been crossed. What I did with it came later. But the anger itself, beta, that was honest."

qa.q: Where did Zubin sit until the bell?
qa.a: He sat behind the school water tank until the bell.

qa.q: What did Zubin feel when the class made ghost noises?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and furious, with burning ears and shaking hands, because Behram had shared his secret and laughed.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point came from Zubin's mother's words?
qa.a: By telling Zubin his anger was right, his mother helped him see it as a sign that trust had been broken, not as something wrong with him.

qa.q: How might Behram have felt when Zubin walked out?
qa.a: Behram may have felt a flash of guilt or awkwardness, realising his joke had deeply hurt his best friend.

grounding: Shows a teenager betrayed by a friend who shared his secret, feeling rage and humiliation, and learning that the anger signals a crossed boundary.
